topics.title: What is Node.js?
topics.summary: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine and libuv that lets you run JavaScript outside the browser.
topics.description:
**Node.js** is not a language and not a framework. It is a **runtime**: a program that can execute JavaScript on your computer or server, outside the browser.

### The main parts
| Part | Role |
|---|---|
| **V8** | Google's JavaScript engine (same as Chrome). Compiles JS to machine code and runs it. |
| **libuv** | A C library that gives Node the **event loop**, a thread pool and cross-platform async I/O (files, DNS, sockets, timers). |
| **Node core (C++ and JS)** | Built-in modules such as `fs`, `http`, `path`, `crypto`, `stream`. |
| **npm** | The package manager that ships with Node and hosts millions of packages. |

### Why Node is fast for I/O work
Your JavaScript runs on **one main thread**. When you ask for something slow (read a file, query a database, call an API), Node hands the job to the operating system or to libuv's thread pool and keeps going. When the result is ready, a **callback** is queued and the event loop runs it. This is called **non-blocking I/O** and it lets one process serve thousands of connections.

### What Node is good at
* REST and GraphQL APIs, real-time apps (chat, notifications), streaming
* Command line tools, build tools, scripts and automation
* Microservices and backends-for-frontends

### What Node is not ideal for
Long CPU-heavy work on the main thread (video encoding, huge JSON crunching) blocks every other request. Use `worker_threads` or another service for that.

### Browser JS vs Node JS
Node has no `window` or `document`, but it has `process`, `fs`, `http`, `Buffer` and more. The language (ES2023+) is the same.
keyPoints: Node = V8 engine + libuv event loop + core modules
Single-threaded JavaScript with non-blocking I/O
Great for I/O-bound apps, weak for CPU-bound work on the main thread
Same JavaScript language as the browser, different APIs
pitfalls: Calling Node "a framework" or "a language" in interviews
Saying Node is "single threaded" without mentioning the libuv thread pool

examples.explanation: There is no window object in Node, so the last line prints false.

examples.title: Run it
examples.code:
$ node hello.js
Hello from Node v24.0.0
Platform: win32
Is browser? false

interview.q: What is Node.js?
interview.a: An open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime built on the V8 engine. It uses an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model (libuv) so a single process can handle many concurrent connections.

interview.q: Is Node.js single-threaded?
interview.a: Your JavaScript code runs on one thread (the event loop), but Node itself uses libuv's thread pool (default 4 threads) for things like file system, DNS lookup, zlib and crypto, and you can add threads with worker_threads.

topics.title: Installing Node and nvm
topics.summary: Install Node from nodejs.org or manage many versions with nvm, fnm or Volta and understand LTS releases.
topics.description:
You can install Node in three common ways.

### 1. Official installer
Download from nodejs.org. Choose the **LTS** (Long Term Support) version for projects. The **Current** line has newest features but is short-lived.

### 2. A version manager (recommended)
Real projects need different Node versions. A version manager lets you switch per project:
* **nvm** (macOS/Linux) and **nvm-windows**
* **fnm** (fast, cross-platform, written in Rust)
* **Volta** (pins the version inside `package.json`)

### Release model
Node ships a new major every six months. Even-numbered majors (20, 22, 24) become **LTS** and receive security fixes for about 30 months. Odd-numbered majors are never LTS. Always use an active LTS line in production.

### Check your setup
`node -v` prints the Node version, `npm -v` prints the npm version, `which node` (or `where node` on Windows) shows which binary runs.

### Pinning a version for a project
Create a `.nvmrc` file containing `22` and run `nvm use`. You can also add `"engines": { "node": ">=20" }` in `package.json` to warn people (and CI) about unsupported versions.

### Tips
* Do not install global packages with `sudo`. A version manager keeps everything in your home folder.
* Keep Node updated: old versions stop receiving security patches.
keyPoints: Use an even-numbered LTS version for production
nvm / fnm / Volta let you switch Node versions per project
.nvmrc and the engines field document the required version
node -v and npm -v verify the installation
pitfalls: Running production on an end-of-life Node version
Installing with sudo and then fighting permission errors

examples.title: nvm workflow
examples.code:
nvm install --lts        # install latest LTS
nvm ls                   # list installed versions
nvm use 22               # switch for this shell
echo "22" > .nvmrc       # pin for the project
nvm use                  # reads .nvmrc
node -v
examples.explanation: On Windows use nvm-windows or fnm; the commands are almost identical.

interview.q: What is LTS in Node.js?
interview.a: Long Term Support. Even-numbered releases get about 30 months of bug and security fixes and are recommended for production, while odd releases are short-lived and meant for trying new features.

interview.q: Why use a version manager?
interview.a: Different projects need different Node versions. A manager installs several versions side by side and switches between them without admin rights or conflicts.

topics.title: REPL and Running Scripts
topics.summary: Use the REPL to experiment and the node command (with flags like --watch and --env-file) to run files.
topics.description:
### The REPL
Type `node` with no arguments to start the **REPL** (Read-Eval-Print Loop). It evaluates each line and prints the result. It is perfect for quick experiments.

Useful REPL features:
* `_` holds the last result
* `.help` lists commands, `.editor` lets you paste multi-line code, `.save file.js` and `.load file.js`
* Tab completion works on objects and built-in modules (which are already available, so `fs` works without `require`)
* `.exit` or Ctrl+D quits

### Running a file
`node app.js` runs a script. The `.js` extension may be left out (`node app`) and `node .` runs the file named in `main` of `package.json`.

### Handy flags
| Flag | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `--watch` | Restart when imported files change |
| `--env-file=.env` | Load environment variables from a file |
| `-e "code"` / `-p "expr"` | Run or print an inline expression |
| `--inspect` | Open the debugger |
| `--check` (`-c`) | Syntax check only |
| `--max-old-space-size=4096` | Raise heap limit (MB) |
| `-r module` / `--import module` | Preload a module |

### Passing arguments
Anything after the file name goes to `process.argv`: `node app.js --port 4000`.

### Running TypeScript
Recent Node versions (22.18+ and 24) can run `.ts` files that use only erasable type syntax with plain `node file.ts` (type stripping, no type checking).

### Exit codes
`0` means success; any other number means failure. Shells and CI use this to detect errors.
keyPoints: node with no args opens the REPL, node file.js runs a script
--watch and --env-file replace nodemon and dotenv for simple cases
Arguments after the file name are available in process.argv
Exit code 0 means success, non-zero means failure
pitfalls: Pasting multi-line code into the REPL without .editor mode
Forgetting that ES module files need .mjs or "type": "module"

examples.title: REPL session
examples.explanation: Built-in modules such as os are auto-loaded in the REPL.

examples.title: Useful one-liners
examples.code:
node -p "process.versions.v8"
node -e "console.log(new Date().toISOString())"
node --watch server.js
node --env-file=.env server.js
node --check broken.js
examples.explanation: -p prints the result of the expression, -e only evaluates it.

interview.q: How do you pass command line arguments to a Node script?
interview.a: Run node app.js a b --flag. They appear in process.argv; index 0 is the node binary, index 1 is the script path and the rest are your arguments. For flags use util.parseArgs.

interview.q: What is the REPL?
interview.a: The Read-Eval-Print Loop, an interactive shell started by running node with no file. It evaluates JavaScript line by line and is useful for quick experiments.

topics.title: npm Basics
topics.summary: npm installs, updates and publishes packages; know install, uninstall, update, ci and the lock file.
topics.description:
**npm** (Node Package Manager) is installed with Node. It downloads packages from the npm registry into `node_modules` and records them in `package.json`.

### Everyday commands
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm init -y` | Create a `package.json` with defaults |
| `npm install express` (`npm i`) | Add a dependency |
| `npm i -D vitest` | Add a **dev** dependency |
| `npm i -g pkg` | Install globally (CLI tools) |
| `npm uninstall pkg` | Remove a package |
| `npm update` | Update within allowed semver ranges |
| `npm outdated` | Show newer versions |
| `npm ls` | Show the dependency tree |
| `npm ci` | Clean, exact install from the lock file (CI and Docker) |
| `npm audit` | Check for known vulnerabilities |

### dependencies vs devDependencies
* `dependencies`: needed at runtime (express, mongoose)
* `devDependencies`: only for development (eslint, vitest, nodemon)
* `npm i --omit=dev` installs only production dependencies

### The lock file
`package-lock.json` records the **exact** version of every package in the tree. Commit it so every teammate and server installs identical code. Use `npm ci` in automation because it fails if the lock file and `package.json` disagree.

### Alternatives
**pnpm** (fast, disk efficient) and **Yarn** do the same job; **Bun** and **Deno** bring their own tools. The concepts are identical.
keyPoints: npm install adds to package.json and node_modules
Use -D for tooling, regular install for runtime packages
Commit package-lock.json; use npm ci in CI and Docker
npm audit checks for known vulnerabilities
pitfalls: Committing node_modules to git
Using npm install instead of npm ci in pipelines, which may change the lock file
Installing a package globally when a local dev dependency would do

examples.title: Starting a project
examples.code:
mkdir hello-node && cd hello-node
npm init -y
npm install express
npm install -D nodemon
npm ls --depth=0
examples.explanation: After this, package.json lists express under dependencies and nodemon under devDependencies.

interview.q: Difference between npm install and npm ci?
interview.a: npm install resolves versions and may update the lock file. npm ci deletes node_modules and installs exactly what the lock file says, failing if it does not match package.json, which makes it fast and reproducible for CI.

interview.q: Why commit package-lock.json?
interview.a: It pins every transitive dependency to an exact version and checksum so builds are reproducible and protected from surprise upgrades.

topics.title: package.json Explained
topics.summary: package.json is the manifest of a Node project: name, version, entry point, scripts, dependencies and module type.
topics.description:
Every Node project has a `package.json`. It describes the project and tells npm what to install.

### Important fields
| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name`, `version` | Identity (needed to publish) |
| `description`, `license`, `author` | Metadata |
| `main` | Entry file for `require('pkg')` |
| `type` | `"module"` makes `.js` files ES modules; `"commonjs"` (default) keeps CommonJS |
| `exports` | Modern, strict map of what a package exposes |
| `scripts` | Named commands run by `npm run` |
| `dependencies` | Runtime packages |
| `devDependencies` | Development only |
| `peerDependencies` | Packages the host app must provide (plugins) |
| `engines` | Required Node/npm versions |
| `bin` | Command names for CLI packages |
| `files` | What gets published |
| `private: true` | Prevents accidental publishing |

### Version ranges
`"express": "^4.19.2"` means "any compatible 4.x.x at or above 4.19.2". See the semver topic for details.

### Typical app manifest
Most applications set `"private": true`, `"type": "module"`, a `start` and a `dev` script and an `engines` field.

### Tip
Edit `package.json` by hand freely, but use `npm install` to change dependencies so the lock file stays in sync.
keyPoints: package.json is the project manifest read by npm and Node
type decides whether .js files are ESM or CommonJS
scripts define reusable commands, dependencies define installs
private: true avoids accidental publishing
engines documents the required Node version
pitfalls: Trailing commas or comments: package.json must be strict JSON
Putting build tools in dependencies and bloating production installs

examples.title: A realistic package.json
examples.explanation: start, dev and test cover the daily workflow.

interview.q: What does the type field do?
interview.a: "type": "module" tells Node to treat .js files in that package as ES modules (import/export). Without it (or with "commonjs") .js files use require/module.exports. .mjs and .cjs always force a mode.

interview.q: dependencies vs devDependencies vs peerDependencies?
interview.a: dependencies are needed at runtime; devDependencies only while developing/building/testing; peerDependencies declare that the consuming app must supply a compatible version, typical for plugins and libraries.

topics.title: npm Scripts
topics.summary: The scripts field turns long commands into short names and supports pre/post hooks and local binaries.
topics.description:
The `scripts` section maps names to shell commands. Run one with `npm run <name>`. Four names are special and need no `run`: `npm start`, `npm test`, `npm stop` and `npm restart`.

### Why use scripts
* Short, memorable commands for the whole team
* They add `node_modules/.bin` to the PATH, so locally installed tools (eslint, vitest) work without a global install
* Same commands in your terminal and in CI

### Hooks
For any script `x`, `prex` runs before it and `postx` after it. `npm run build` first runs `prebuild`. Special lifecycle hooks: `prepare` (after install, used by Husky) and `prepublishOnly`.

### Passing arguments
Use `--` to forward arguments: `npm run dev -- --port 4000` ends up as `--port 4000` for the script.

### Chaining
* `a && b` runs b only if a succeeds
* `a ; b` runs both (not on Windows cmd)
* Packages such as `npm-run-all2` or `concurrently` run scripts in parallel
* `npm run build --workspaces` runs across a monorepo

### Environment variables
Set variables with `cross-env NODE_ENV=production node app.js` for Windows compatibility, or use `node --env-file`.

### Useful extras
`npm run` lists all scripts. Inside scripts, `npm_package_name` and `npm_package_version` are available as env vars.
keyPoints: Scripts are named shell commands run with npm run name
start and test can be run as npm start / npm test
node_modules/.bin is on the PATH inside scripts
pre and post prefixes create hooks, -- forwards arguments
pitfalls: Writing shell syntax that breaks on Windows (use cross-platform tools)
Forgetting the -- when forwarding flags to the underlying command

examples.title: Scripts with hooks
examples.explanation: npm run build runs prebuild, build, postbuild in order.

interview.q: How do you pass flags to an npm script?
interview.a: Put -- before them: npm run dev -- --port 4000. Everything after -- is appended to the script's command.

interview.q: Why can scripts run tools that are not installed globally?
interview.a: npm prepends node_modules/.bin to PATH while running scripts, so locally installed executables are found automatically.

topics.title: Semantic Versioning
topics.summary: Versions look like MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; the ^ and ~ symbols control which updates npm accepts.
topics.description:
npm packages follow **semver**: `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, for example `4.18.2`.

* **PATCH** (4.18.**3**): bug fixes, nothing breaks
* **MINOR** (4.**19**.0): new backwards-compatible features
* **MAJOR** (**5**.0.0): breaking changes

### Range symbols in package.json
| Range | Accepts | Example result |
|---|---|---|
| `4.18.2` | exactly this version | 4.18.2 |
| `^4.18.2` | same major, at or above | 4.18.2 up to < 5.0.0 |
| `~4.18.2` | same minor, at or above | 4.18.2 up to < 4.19.0 |
| `>=4 <6` | explicit range | 4.x or 5.x |
| `*` or `latest` | anything | dangerous |

### Special case: 0.x versions
For `^0.2.3` only patch updates are accepted (`< 0.3.0`) because 0.x is considered unstable.

### Pre-releases
`2.0.0-beta.1` sorts before `2.0.0`. Tags such as `next` or `beta` are used for early access: `npm i pkg@beta`.

### Why it matters
`^` gives you automatic bug fixes, but the lock file is what actually stops surprise upgrades. Updating a **major** version requires reading the changelog.

### Checking
`npm outdated` shows current, wanted (within range) and latest versions. `npm view express versions` lists all.
keyPoints: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking.feature.fix
^ allows minor and patch updates, ~ allows only patch
Caret on 0.x versions behaves more strictly
The lock file freezes the exact versions that were installed
pitfalls: Assuming minor updates can never break anything (maintainers make mistakes)
Using * or latest in dependencies

examples.title: Range behaviour
examples.explanation: Ranges are resolved by npm at install time, then frozen in package-lock.json.

interview.q: What does ^ mean in package.json?
interview.a: Accept any version that does not change the left-most non-zero digit. ^1.2.3 means >=1.2.3 <2.0.0, ^0.2.3 means >=0.2.3 <0.3.0.

interview.q: When does a package bump the major version?
interview.a: When it makes a backwards-incompatible change such as removing or renaming an API, so consumers must opt in and review the migration notes.

topics.title: npx and Running Package Binaries
topics.summary: npx runs a package's command without a global install, perfect for scaffolding tools and one-off scripts.
topics.description:
**npx** ships with npm. It runs a command from a package, using the local `node_modules/.bin` if the package is installed there, or downloading it temporarily if not.

### Common uses
* **Scaffolding**: `npx create-vite@latest my-app`, `npx create-next-app`
* **One-off tools**: `npx kill-port 3000`, `npx serve .`
* **Using a local binary**: `npx eslint .` after `npm i -D eslint`
* **Trying a specific version**: `npx typescript@5.4 --version`

### How it decides
1. Look in the local project's `node_modules/.bin`
2. Look in the PATH
3. Otherwise download into a cache and run it (npx asks first for unknown packages)

### Flags
* `-y` or `--yes` skip the install prompt (useful in CI)
* `-p pkg1 -p pkg2 command` use several packages
* `--no-install` fail instead of downloading

### Related tools
* `npm exec` is the underlying command
* `npm create vite@latest` is shorthand for `npx create-vite@latest`
* `pnpm dlx` and `yarn dlx` do the same in other managers

### Security note
Running `npx some-package` executes code from the internet with your permissions. Check the package name (typos are used by attackers) and prefer well known packages.
keyPoints: npx executes a package binary without a permanent install
It prefers local binaries over downloads
Great for scaffolding with create-* packages
Only run packages you trust: it executes arbitrary code
pitfalls: Typo-squatting: npx create-raect-app may be malicious
Forgetting @latest and scaffolding from a cached old version

examples.title: npx examples
examples.code:
npx create-vite@latest my-app --template react
npx serve ./public
npx --yes http-server -p 8080
npx eslint src
examples.explanation: The first two download the tool on demand; the last uses your local install.

interview.q: What is the difference between npm install -g and npx?
interview.a: A global install keeps a permanent, possibly outdated copy on your machine. npx runs the package on demand (cached, or the local version), so you always control the version and avoid polluting global space.

interview.q: What is npm exec?
interview.a: The npm command that npx is built on. It runs a binary from a local or remote package, with npx being its convenient front end.

topics.title: node_modules and Dependency Resolution
topics.summary: node_modules holds installed packages in a nested tree; learn how lookup works, why it gets huge and how to manage it.
topics.description:
`node_modules` is the folder where npm places every package your project depends on, including the dependencies of your dependencies (**transitive** dependencies).

### How lookup works
When you write `require('lodash')` or `import 'lodash'`, Node looks in:
1. `./node_modules/lodash`
2. `../node_modules/lodash`
3. `../../node_modules/lodash` ... up to the filesystem root

This is why a package installed in the parent folder is visible to child folders.

### Flat tree and duplicates
npm tries to **hoist** (flatten) shared packages to the top level to avoid duplication. If two packages need incompatible versions, one is nested inside the other's own `node_modules`.

### Why it is heavy
A simple app can pull in hundreds of packages. This is the reason for:
* `.gitignore` containing `node_modules/`
* pnpm, which stores one copy globally and links it
* Docker layers that install dependencies before copying source

### Cleaning up
* Delete `node_modules` and run `npm ci` to fix strange errors
* `npm dedupe` merges duplicates, `npm prune` removes extraneous packages
* `npm ls package-name` shows who depends on a package and which version
* `npm explain pkg` explains why a package is installed

### Never edit inside
Changes in `node_modules` are lost on the next install. Use `patch-package` or fork the library if you need a fix.
keyPoints: node_modules contains direct and transitive dependencies
Node walks up parent folders to find a package
npm hoists shared versions, nesting only when versions conflict
Never commit it, never edit it; reinstall with npm ci
pitfalls: Committing node_modules to version control
Hand-editing a library inside node_modules
Copying node_modules between operating systems (native modules break)

examples.title: Inspect the tree
examples.code:
npm ls express            # who uses express and which version
npm explain debug         # why is "debug" installed?
npm ls --all | wc -l      # size of the whole tree
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json && npm install   # nuclear option
examples.explanation: Prefer npm ci when you only want to restore the lock file state.

interview.q: How does Node find a package imported by name?
interview.a: It looks for node_modules/<name> in the current file's directory, then each parent directory in turn up to the root, and uses the package's main or exports entry.

interview.q: Why is node_modules in .gitignore?
interview.a: It is large, reproducible from package.json plus the lock file, and may contain OS-specific binaries, so only the manifest and lock file are committed.

topics.title: Global Objects and Variables
topics.summary: globalThis, process, console, Buffer, timers, URL, fetch and module-scoped variables like __dirname.
topics.description:
Node exposes a set of **globals** that need no import.

### True globals
| Name | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `globalThis` | The global object (works everywhere, replaces `global` / `window`) |
| `process` | Info and control of the running process |
| `console` | Logging |
| `Buffer` | Binary data |
| `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate`, `queueMicrotask` | Scheduling |
| `URL`, `URLSearchParams`, `TextEncoder`, `TextDecoder` | Web standard utilities |
| `fetch`, `Request`, `Response`, `Headers`, `FormData` | HTTP client (undici) |
| `AbortController`, `structuredClone`, `performance`, `crypto` (Web Crypto) | Modern web APIs |

### Module-scoped variables (CommonJS only)
Each CommonJS file is wrapped in a function, so `require`, `module`, `exports`, `__filename` and `__dirname` are **local to the file**, not real globals.

### ES module equivalents
ESM has no `__dirname`. Use:
* `import.meta.url` (file URL of the current module)
* `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename` (Node 20.11+)
* `fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)` for older versions

### Variables declared at the top level
`var x = 1` in a Node file does **not** create `globalThis.x`, because the file is a module with its own scope. This differs from browser scripts.

### Avoid polluting globals
Assigning `globalThis.config = ...` makes hidden dependencies and bugs. Export from a module instead.
keyPoints: globalThis is the universal global object in Node and browsers
process, Buffer, console, timers, fetch and URL are available without imports
__dirname and __filename exist only in CommonJS; ESM uses import.meta.dirname
Top-level var does not create a global in Node
pitfalls: Using __dirname inside an ES module (ReferenceError)
Storing shared state on globalThis

examples.title: Globals at work
examples.explanation: Save as a .cjs file to try the last two lines.

examples.title: Path of the current file in ESM
examples.explanation: Always build file paths from the current file, not from process.cwd().

interview.q: Are __dirname and require globals?
interview.a: No. In CommonJS every file is wrapped in a function that receives exports, require, module, __filename and __dirname as parameters, so they are module-scoped. ES modules do not have them.

interview.q: What is globalThis?
interview.a: A standard reference to the global object that works in every JS environment (window in browsers, global in Node, self in workers).

topics.title: CommonJS vs ES Modules
topics.summary: require/module.exports versus import/export: syntax, loading behaviour, interop and how to choose.
topics.description:
Node supports two module systems.

| | CommonJS (CJS) | ES Modules (ESM) |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax | `require()`, `module.exports` | `import`, `export` |
| Loading | Synchronous | Asynchronous, statically analysed |
| File types | `.js` (default), `.cjs` | `.mjs`, or `.js` with `"type": "module"` |
| Top-level `await` | No | Yes |
| `__dirname` | Yes | No (use `import.meta.dirname`) |
| Strict mode | Optional | Always |
| Live bindings | Copies of values | Live read-only views |

### Enabling ESM
Put `"type": "module"` in `package.json`, or name files `.mjs`.

### Interop rules
* ESM can `import` CommonJS (module.exports becomes the default export)
* CommonJS `require()` of an ES module is supported in current Node versions (22.12+ and 24) when the module has no top-level `await`; before that you needed `await import()`
* Dynamic `import('./x.js')` works in both systems and returns a promise

### Which should you pick?
New projects: **ESM**. It is the language standard, supports top-level await and tree shaking, and is what browsers use. CommonJS remains everywhere in older code and docs, so you must read both.

### Named vs default
CJS: `module.exports = { add }`. ESM: `export function add() {}` or `export default`. Mixing `module.exports` and `export` in one file is an error.

### Import specifiers
ESM requires the **file extension** for relative imports (`./utils.js`), unlike many bundlers. Built-ins use the `node:` prefix: `import fs from 'node:fs'`.
keyPoints: CJS: require and module.exports, synchronous; ESM: import and export, async and static
Enable ESM with "type": "module" or the .mjs extension
ESM needs file extensions in relative imports and has no __dirname
Use dynamic import() to load ESM from CJS (or require(esm) on new Node)
Prefer ESM for new code
pitfalls: Forgetting the .js extension in a relative ESM import
Using require in a "type": "module" package (ReferenceError)
Mixing module.exports and export in one file

examples.title: Same module in both styles
examples.explanation: The two files at the top are CommonJS, the two at the bottom use ES modules.

interview.q: require vs import: key differences?
interview.a: require is a synchronous function evaluated at runtime and returns a copy of module.exports. import is static syntax, resolved before execution, asynchronous, gives live bindings and enables tree shaking and top-level await.

interview.q: How do you use __dirname in ESM?
interview.a: Use import.meta.dirname (Node 20.11+), or path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)) on older versions.

topics.title: Module Resolution and Caching
topics.summary: How Node resolves relative paths, node_modules names, index files and exports maps, and why modules are cached.
topics.description:
### Resolution order for `require(x)`
1. **Core module** (`fs`, `node:path`) always wins
2. **Relative or absolute path** (`./a`, `../a`, `/a`): try the exact file, then add `.js`, `.json`, `.node`; then treat it as a directory (`package.json` `main`, then `index.js`)
3. **Bare name** (`lodash`): walk up through every `node_modules` folder

`require.resolve('x')` prints the file that would be loaded without running it.

### The exports map
Modern packages use `"exports"` in `package.json` to declare their public entry points. Anything not listed cannot be imported (deep imports like `pkg/lib/internal.js` throw `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`). It also allows conditions:

`{ "exports": { "import": "./esm/index.js", "require": "./cjs/index.cjs" } }`

### Caching
A module runs **once**. The result is stored in `require.cache` (CJS) or the module map (ESM); later imports get the same object. This makes modules natural **singletons** (a db connection, a config object).

### Circular dependencies
If `a` requires `b` and `b` requires `a`, `b` receives the **partially filled** `exports` of `a`. Symptoms: `undefined` imports. Fix by restructuring, moving shared code to a third module or requiring lazily inside functions.

### ESM differences
ESM does not search extensions or `index.js` for relative imports; you must write full paths. Use `import.meta.resolve()` to resolve a specifier.

### Aliases
Node supports `"imports": { "#utils/*": "./src/utils/*.js" }` for private aliases starting with `#`.

examples.title: Caching is real
examples.explanation: Because the file ran only once, both variables reference the same exports object.

interview.q: Why does requiring the same module twice not re-run it?
interview.a: Node caches the module by resolved filename in require.cache after the first load, so later require calls return the cached exports. This makes modules behave like singletons.

interview.q: What is the package.json exports field for?
interview.a: It defines a package's public API: the only paths consumers may import, optionally per condition (import, require, node, default), which prevents deep imports into internals.

topics.title: Built-in Modules Overview
topics.summary: A map of the core modules shipped with Node and the node: import prefix.
topics.description:
Node ships a standard library. You never install these; just import them with the **`node:` prefix** (clear, and avoids clashing with npm packages of the same name).

### Map of the important ones
| Area | Modules |
|---|---|
| Files and paths | `fs`, `fs/promises`, `path`, `os`, `url` |
| Network | `http`, `https`, `http2`, `net`, `dgram`, `dns`, `tls` |
| Async tools | `events`, `stream`, `stream/promises`, `timers/promises`, `async_hooks` |
| Data | `buffer`, `zlib`, `string_decoder`, `querystring` |
| Security | `crypto` |
| Processes and threads | `child_process`, `cluster`, `worker_threads`, `process` |
| Utilities | `util`, `assert`, `readline`, `perf_hooks`, `diagnostics_channel` |
| Testing and storage | `test` (`node:test`), `sqlite` (`node:sqlite`) |
| Diagnostics | `inspector`, `v8`, `repl`, `trace_events` |

### How to import
CommonJS: `const fs = require('node:fs');`
ESM: `import fs from 'node:fs';` or named: `import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';`

### Promise versions
Many callback APIs have promise twins: `node:fs/promises`, `node:timers/promises`, `node:dns/promises`, `node:readline/promises`, `node:stream/promises`. Prefer them with `async/await`.

### Discover more
In the REPL, `require('node:module').builtinModules` lists all of them. The official docs at nodejs.org/api document each module with stability markers (Stable, Experimental, Deprecated).

### Stability index
Check the stability badge: *Experimental* APIs can change in any release. Avoid them in critical production code unless you pin the Node version.
keyPoints: Core modules need no installation, only an import
Use the node: prefix for clarity and safety
Prefer the promise-based variants with async/await
Check each API's stability index in the docs
pitfalls: Installing an npm package with the same name as a core module
Depending on Experimental APIs without pinning the Node version

interview.q: Why import with the node: prefix?
interview.a: It makes it explicit that the module is built in, prevents a malicious or accidental npm package from shadowing it, and some newer modules (like node:test and node:sqlite) are only available with the prefix.

interview.q: Name five core modules and what they do.
interview.a: fs reads and writes files, path handles file paths, http creates servers and clients, events provides EventEmitter, crypto offers hashing and encryption; also stream, os, util, child_process.
